html:
Khoisan is an umbrella name for the peoples of southern Africa who speak click languages and who lived there before Bantu-speaking farmers and European settlers arrived. The map shows their lands across most of southern Africa from 3000 BCE to 1500.

The name joins two ways of life:

  • the San, hunter-gatherers who lived in small bands, hunted with poisoned arrows and gathered plants, roots and water-filled melons;
  • the Khoekhoe, herders of sheep and later cattle, who lived in larger groups and moved with their herds.

The San and their ancestors are among the oldest continuous populations on earth, with genetic lineages that split from other humans very early. They painted and engraved many thousands of images of animals, people and trance rituals on rocks across the region.

Herding came later. Sheep, and then cattle, spread south from East Africa, and herders reached the Cape around the start of the common era. From about the same time the Bantu expansion brought iron-using farmers into the wetter east and north. Over many centuries farmers and Khoisan traded, married and fought; the Xhosa and Zulu languages took their click sounds from Khoisan neighbours. The Khoisan held on mostly in the dry west, from the Cape to the Kalahari, where crops grew poorly.

When the Dutch settled the Cape in 1652, the Khoekhoe there lost land and cattle in wars and to smallpox, and many were forced into labour in the Cape Colony. San bands survive today in Namibia and Botswana.
